title: Reading an equilibrium: Q, K and Le Châtelier
promptMarkdown:
Dinitrogen tetroxide dissociates: $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2 NO2(g)}$. Take $K = 0.146$ at 298 K with a reference pressure of 1 bar (this is the reciprocal of the value the lecture 18 notes use for the reverse reaction), and treat the forward reaction as endothermic. $R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$.

1. A vessel at 298 K contains $P(\ce{N2O4}) = 0.500$ bar and $P(\ce{NO2}) = 0.100$ bar. Compute $Q$ and say which direction the reaction runs.
2. A different rigid vessel, held at 298 K with ideal gases throughout, initially contains 1.000 bar of $\ce{N2O4}$ and no $\ce{NO2}$. Set up an ICE table and compute the equilibrium partial pressures; check them by substituting back.
3. Compute $\Delta G^\circ$ for the reaction as written at 298 K.
4. Predict, with a reason stated in terms of $Q$ and $K$, the effect on the equilibrium amount of $\ce{NO2}$ of: (a) compressing the equilibrium mixture to half its volume at constant temperature; (b) raising the temperature; (c) adding argon at constant volume; (d) adding a catalyst. In each case say whether $K$ changes.
hintLadder: $Q$ has the same form as $K$ but uses the pressures you have now: $Q = P(\ce{NO2})^2/P(\ce{N2O4})$ with pressures in bar.

At fixed volume and temperature, partial pressures change in the stoichiometric proportions. Let $x$ bar of $\ce{N2O4}$ dissociate; then $P(\ce{NO2}) = 2x$ and $P(\ce{N2O4}) = 1.000 - x$. The resulting quadratic has one positive root.
$\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ with $R$ in J; convert to kJ at the end and keep the sign.
For each stress ask: does it change $Q$ (then the system moves back towards the unchanged $K$) or does it change $K$ itself (only temperature does)?

deterministicChecks.description: claiming that K changes with pressure, volume, inert gas or a catalyst

criteria.criterion: Q = 0.100²/0.500 = 0.0200 < K, so the forward reaction runs (more NO2).

criteria.criterion: (a) compression raises Q above K, shift to N2O4, less NO2, K unchanged; (b) heating raises K for the endothermic forward reaction, more NO2; (c) argon at constant volume changes no partial pressure, no shift, K unchanged; (d) a catalyst changes neither Q nor K, equilibrium reached faster.

checkExamples.label: correct answer
checkExamples.text: Q = 0.100^2/0.500 = 0.0200, below K = 0.146, so the reaction runs forward. ICE: N2O4 1.000 - x, NO2 2x; (2x)^2/(1.000 - x) = 0.146 gives 4x^2 + 0.146x - 0.146 = 0, x = 0.1737, so P(NO2) = 0.347 bar and P(N2O4) = 0.826 bar; check 0.347^2/0.826 = 0.146. ΔG° = -8.314 x 298 x ln(0.146) = +4770 J/mol = +4.77 kJ/mol. (a) Halving the volume doubles both pressures, Q doubles and exceeds K, so the system shifts towards N2O4 and the NO2 amount falls; K is unchanged. (b) Heating raises K for the endothermic forward reaction, so more NO2. (c) Argon at constant volume changes no partial pressure: no shift, K unchanged. (d) A catalyst changes neither Q nor K; equilibrium is reached faster.

checkExamples.label: K treated as pressure dependent
checkExamples.text: Q = 0.2 so the reaction runs backwards. K changes when the pressure increases, so compressing gives a new equilibrium constant, and a catalyst increases K.
